root.name: St. George Defense: Polish Variation
root.moves: 1. e4 a6 2. d4 b5 3. Nf3 Bb7 4. Bd3 e6

overview: White has a broad e4-d4 centre against Black's flank set-up (...a6, ...b5, ...Bb7, ...e6). White develops with Bd3, O-O, c4 or Nbd2/Nc3 and tries to use the extra space; Black hits the centre with ...Nf6 and ...c5. Play is flexible and strategic, and a tricky position for White to convert.

white_ideas.idea: Castle and support the centre with c4 or Nbd2 and Re1
Hold e4 and d4, then push e5 when Black has committed pieces
Attack b5 and the queenside with Bxb5 tricks once ...a6 is loosened

black_ideas.idea: Use the b7 bishop on the long diagonal against e4

typical_structures.structure: White pawns on d4 and e4 against Black's ...a6/...b5/...e6 set-up
After ...c5, a Sicilian-like centre with an open c-file

character.notes: Neither side commits to forcing play; White's space meets Black's flank counterplay.

gambit.notes: No material is given up on purpose in 1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 e6.

soundness.notes: Black's hypermodern set-up is playable though White is slightly better; neither side takes a real risk.

structure.notes: The centre is undecided until Black plays ...c5 or ...d5 or White plays e5.

approach.notes: The St George is seldom chosen by strong players and is played mainly for surprise.

level.notes: Black must know how to attack White's centre; White needs sound centre play rather than memorised lines.

sublines_that_differ.name: Basman 4...Nf6
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 a6 2. d4 b5 3. Nf3 Bb7 4. Bd3 Nf6
sublines_that_differ.how: Black plays more directly with ...Nf6 and White can tempt with e5 or Bxb5 axb5 Nxb5.
